questions.question: A 62-year-old without lung-cancer symptoms smoked one pack daily for 25 years and quit 10 years ago. Which action aligns with U.S. screening recommendations?
choices: Discuss annual low-dose CT screening and its benefits and harms
Order a diagnostic bronchoscopy for every former smoker
Wait until symptoms appear before discussing any prevention
Use a routine chest x-ray as the recommended screening test
questions.explanation: The person is 50–80 years old, has at least 20 pack-years, and quit less than 15 years ago. Annual LDCT with shared decision-making is the recommended screening approach for eligible asymptomatic adults.

questions.question: A client reports new hemoptysis, persistent cough, and weight loss but does not meet LDCT screening criteria. What is the best RN response?
choices: Arrange timely diagnostic evaluation of the symptoms
Explain that no evaluation is needed because screening criteria are not met
Schedule screening LDCT next year and reassess then
Attribute the symptoms to smoking without assessment
questions.explanation: Screening criteria apply to asymptomatic people. Hemoptysis and progressive constitutional or respiratory symptoms require diagnostic assessment regardless of screening eligibility.

questions.question: A chest CT identifies a suspicious lung mass. Which information is most important before assuming a specific cancer treatment plan?
choices: Tissue diagnosis, extent of disease, relevant biomarkers, functional status, and client goals
The CT appearance alone
The client's age alone
Whether the client has ever had a chest x-ray
questions.explanation: Pathology, stage, molecular features when appropriate, cardiopulmonary reserve, performance status, and preferences guide individualized treatment; an image alone is insufficient.

questions.question: After bronchoscopy with topical anesthetic and sedation, a client asks for water. What should the RN do?
choices: Assess airway and recovery criteria, and withhold oral intake until protective swallowing reflexes return per protocol
Give water immediately to soothe the throat
Offer a full meal before reassessing mental status
Assume the gag reflex is normal because the client can speak
questions.explanation: Topical anesthesia and sedation increase aspiration risk. The RN verifies recovery and protective reflexes according to procedure orders and policy before oral intake.

questions.question: Which new finding after transthoracic lung biopsy most strongly suggests a complication requiring prompt assessment?
choices: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, falling saturation, and diminished breath sounds
Mild fatigue with stable oxygenation and breath sounds
A request for a blanket
An unchanged baseline cough
questions.explanation: This acute cluster raises concern for pneumothorax or another respiratory complication after biopsy. Assess the client and escalate rather than waiting for routine follow-up.

questions.question: After lobectomy, which plan best supports respiratory recovery while reducing avoidable complications?
choices: Provide ordered analgesia with sedation monitoring, pulmonary hygiene, assisted early mobility, and VTE prevention
Keep the client immobile and avoid coughing until discharge
Withhold pain treatment so respiratory rate stays high
Clamp every chest drain during ambulation regardless of the operation
questions.explanation: Adequate but safe analgesia enables deep breathing, coughing, and mobility. Postoperative drainage and activity follow the specific surgery and orders; routine clamping is unsafe.

questions.question: A client with a thoracic tumor develops facial and neck swelling, distended chest veins, and worsening dyspnea when supine. Which complication is most concerning?
choices: Superior vena cava syndrome with possible airway compromise
Expected postoperative edema
Simple dehydration
An isolated skin allergy without respiratory risk
questions.explanation: Upper-body venous congestion and positional dyspnea suggest superior vena cava obstruction. New respiratory distress or neurologic changes require urgent evaluation.

questions.question: A person with lung cancer develops new severe back pain, leg weakness, and urinary retention. What should the RN do first?
choices: Treat possible spinal cord compression as time-sensitive and urgently escalate
Schedule a routine follow-up in several weeks
Encourage walking alone to test strength
Assume the symptoms are anxiety until a scheduled scan
questions.explanation: New back pain with motor and bladder changes can indicate metastatic spinal cord compression. Prompt neurologic assessment and urgent specialist escalation help protect function.

questions.question: A client receiving immunotherapy reports a new persistent cough, dyspnea, and lower oxygen saturation. Which possibility must be considered?
choices: Treatment-related pneumonitis that needs prompt evaluation
Proof that the tumor is responding normally
An expected effect that never needs reporting
A reason to stop all assessment once infection is excluded
questions.explanation: New respiratory symptoms during or after immunotherapy can reflect pneumonitis, infection, cancer progression, or another cause. The RN promptly reports and assesses the change.

questions.question: A client with small-cell lung cancer has low serum sodium and increasing confusion. Which follow-up best evaluates risk and response?
choices: Trend neurologic status and sodium, protect against seizures as indicated, and urgently report worsening symptoms
Assume confusion is unrelated to the sodium level
Encourage unrestricted water intake without reviewing the plan
Delay reassessment until the next chemotherapy cycle
questions.explanation: Small-cell lung cancer may be associated with SIADH. Symptomatic hyponatremia can progress to seizures and impaired consciousness, requiring close neurologic and laboratory follow-up.
